See ibid., § 4: “Although Magister primus (Aristotle) was a man of great merit and eminent authority, a profound mind with perfect powers of philosophical reasoning, it is nevertheless unacceptable to praise him so extravagantly that those who were his masters are belittled—namely, the men who produced sacred books and were prophet-legislators, such as Agathodaimôn, Hermes, Asclepius, and others.” Shahrazôrî comments at length; Qotboddîn Shîrâzî does little more here than reproduce his explanation: “Agathodaimôn, that is, Seth, son of Adam (above, p. 25, n. 26); Hermes, that is, the prophet Idrîs (or Enoch); and Asclepius, the servant and disciple of Hermes, who was the father of the philosophers (hokamâ’) and physicians. All three were eminent prophets (anbiâ’) who combined the excellence of prophecy with philosophical wisdom. They were therefore capable of assembling the body of theosophical teaching (tadwîn al-hikmat) and initiating others into philosophy. The author names all three here either because Aristotle received wisdom from Plato, Plato from Socrates, Socrates from Pythagoras, Pythagoras from Empedocles, and so on back to the two Imams Agathodaimôn and Hermes—and the master of your master is also your master—or because Aristotle himself relied on their books and accounts of their teaching. They were therefore his masters in reality as well. Had Avicenna shown the least fairness, he would have acknowledged that Aristotle owed the sources he developed to Plato.” Both commentators go on to praise Plato with enthusiasm as a contemplator of divine Beauty, “an eminent theologian who was by no means deficient in rational dialectic, as Avicenna claimed. Moreover, most of his books have never been translated into Arabic; they have even been lost and disappeared.” See Op. metaph. I, pp. 304–305. This long quotation, which we have abridged, expresses a strong sense of “prophetic philosophy”: philosophy begins with prophet-sages (Empedocles, Hermes, Agathodaimôn). It also testifies to the “Platonic revival” brought about within Islam—or at least Iranian Islam—by Sohrawardî’s work. ↩

Ibid., p. 12. Even during the ghaybat, the occultation or concealment of the “Pole,” the Pole remains the Pole. The word barzakh denotes anything that acts as a screen or barrier, anything that stands “between two.” In ordinary theological usage it has an end-times meaning: the in-between world, the mundus imaginalis (the city of Jâbarsâ), the world and intermediate state between this life and the Great Resurrection (Qiyâmat Kobrâ). In Sohrawardî’s vocabulary it denotes anything that blocks light, whether in the elemental or the astral world. Etymologically, barzakh or farsakh, as a unit of distance, is thought to derive from the Greek παρασάγγης (parasang). ↩

On this cosmic drama, see our Trilogie ismaélienne, index under “the drama in Heaven.” In a lengthy gloss that we cannot examine here (Gloss 354 on § 126, p. 120), Mollâ Sadrâ develops the idea that acts of being, individual existences, contain a certain incapacity, weakness or deficiency in the order of “descent” (nozûl). Darkness arises from this deficiency as the negation of Light. This deficiency belongs to existence accidentally, not essentially. Secondary matter and material embodiment suffer from a weakness inherent in their act of existing; that weakness is their very opacity. But, according to Sadrâ, one can escape the dualism (thanawiya) that posits Ahriman’s necessary and demonic existence only by adopting a metaphysics of being that gives priority to esse—the act of existing—over essence or whatness. One can speak of a degradation in the act of existing; if instead one speaks of a degradation of essences, a dark essence will ultimately demand a dark first principle. This is the great question at the heart of Mollâ Sadrâ’s philosophy. We refer here to our edition and translation of his Livre des pénétrations métaphysiques (Bibliothèque Iranienne, vol. 10). ↩

This is the anonymous treatise mentioned in our Prolegomena I, p. 50, n. 79, entitled Risâla fî’l-mothol al-‘aqlîya al-aflâtûnîya wa’l-mo’allaqa al-khayâlîya (Treatise on Platonic Archetypes of an Intelligible Nature and Suspended Images of an Imaginal Nature). It was subsequently edited by ’Abdurrahman Badawî under the title Ideae Platonicae, Cairo, 1947. Its title already makes the essential distinction between the Idea as archetype at the level of intellectual intuition and Intelligence (the world of Jabarût), and the Idea at the level of imaginative perception and the world of the Soul (the world of Malakût). “Suspended” means that these image-Ideas do not inhere in matter, as, for example, a brown colour inheres in a piece of wood. Sohrawardî never confused the two; his understanding of the Platonic Ideas, however, follows a tradition different from that of the falâsifa (the philosophers of the Islamic Peripatetic tradition). ↩
